subject: How can I use "brms" to compute a Bayes Factor representing the probability that H0 is true?

messages.author: bafbff7f5abd72d1
messages.subject: How can I use "brms" to compute a Bayes Factor representing the probability that H0 is true?
parts:
I have a simple model in brms:

prior<-c(set_prior("cauchy(0, 2.5)",class = "b", coef = ""),set_prior("cauchy(0, 10)", class = "Intercept", coef = ""))
m1<-brm(DV~IV+(1|Subject), data = data, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 20

The DV is a continuous variable; the IV is a dichotomous variable.

I would like to compute the Bayes Factor that the IV has no effect on the DV (i.e., that its coefficient is equal to 0).

I thought I might do this like this:

h1 <- hypothesis(data, "IV = 0")

However it returns an NA for the evidence ratio:

Hypothesis Tests for class b:
             Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Evid.Ratio Star
(IV) =       0     -0.2      0.46    -1.12     0.72         NA     
---
'*': The expected value under the hypothesis lies outside the 95% CI.

Is my best option to compute a model without the variable of interest, and then do:

bayes_factor(fit1, fit2)

Is this the same as asking: what is the Bayes Factor that IV = 0?
I'm curious if this is still "Bayesian" as it seems not that different from regular model comparisons, would love to hear about the difference.

Is there another way?

Thanks!

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] How can I use "brms" to compute a Bayes Factor representing the probability that H0 is true?
parts:
Yes, this is the same (up to numerical error). Moreover, bayes_factor() is more reliable than hypothesis() in case of diffiult priors. For instance, the cauchy() prior may cause problems for hypothesis().

Please see ?hypothesis for explanation why Evid.Ratio is NA by default.

2018-03-02 2:43 GMT+01:00 David Sidhu <dms...@gmail.com>:
I have a simple model in brms:

prior<-c(set_prior("cauchy(0, 2.5)",class = "b", coef = ""),set_prior("cauchy(0, 10)", class = "Intercept", coef = ""))
m1<-brm(DV~IV+(1|Subject), data = data, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 20

The DV is a continuous variable; the IV is a dichotomous variable.

I would like to compute the Bayes Factor that the IV has no effect on the DV (i.e., that its coefficient is equal to 0).

I thought I might do this like this:

h1 <- hypothesis(data, "IV = 0")

However it returns an NA for the evidence ratio:

Hypothesis Tests for class b:
             Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Evid.Ratio Star
(IV) =       0     -0.2      0.46    -1.12     0.72         NA     
---
'*': The expected value under the hypothesis lies outside the 95% CI.

Is my best option to compute a model without the variable of interest, and then do:

bayes_factor(fit1, fit2)

Is this the same as asking: what is the Bayes Factor that IV = 0?
I'm curious if this is still "Bayesian" as it seems not that different from regular model comparisons, would love to hear about the difference.

Is there another way?

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] How can I use "brms" to compute a Bayes Factor representing the probability that H0 is true?
parts: > Will provide P(D|H1) / P(D|H0)? (In this case H1: b_IV ≠ 0; H0: b_IV = 0).
This is correct. If you are interested in posterior probabilities of models / hypothesis, try out method post_prob()
2018-03-09 2:54 GMT+01:00 David Sidhu <dms...@gmail.com>:

Am I correct that running this:


m1<-brm(DV~IV+(1|Subject), data = data, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 20, save_all_pars = TRUE)
m0<-brm(DV~(1|Subject), data = data, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 20, save_all_pars = TRUE)

test<-bayes_factor(h1, h0)

Will provide P(D|H1) / P(D|H0)? (In this case H1: b_IV ≠ 0; H0: b_IV = 0).

Is there a way to instead compute P(H0|D)? Wagenmakers et al. (2010) suggest that calculating BFH0/(BFH0 + 1) provides the probability of P(H0|D). However, the results don't seem to line up with my results when BF is calculated with the above method. For instance, take the following posterior distribution:


The above method gives P(H0|D) = .70. Just based on an eye test, this doesn't seem to be true; however, maybe I am making a mistake and that is a reasonable probability?

Hi Paul

One more quick question. I seem to have found that Bayes Factors traditionally compares a posterior distribution to a prior distribution within the same model. However, we are talking about comparing two models. Do you mind explaining how the latter approach approximates the former?

Thanks!

On Saturday, 3 March 2018 02:24:59 UTC-7, Paul Buerkner wrote:
I think the blog post you mention is a good introduction to understanding Bayes factors.

2018-03-02 20:38 GMT+01:00 David Sidhu <dms...@gmail.com>:
Perfect, thanks so much! So it sounds like the best way to test the null hypothesis is to compare a model with and without a variable of interest, for instance:

m1<-brm(DV~IV+(1|Subject), data = data, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 20, save_all_pars = TRUE)
m0<-brm(DV~(1|Subject), data = data, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 1000, iter = 2000, chains = 20, save_all_pars = TRUE)

test<-bayes_factor(h1, h0)

Also, as a side note is this a good guideline for interpretation? https://www.r-bloggers.com/what-does-a-bayes-factor-feel-like/
